For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\frac{1}{Q}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=g(x)
$$

where $g(x)$ is independent of $y,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(x)=\operatorname{exp}⁡(\int g(x)\,\text{d}x)
$$

where $\operatorname{exp}⁡(x)$ denotes the exponential function ${e}^{x}.$

First, we rewrite our equation in differential form: 

$$
(2-3y)\,\text{d}x+\text{d}y=0
$$

Let's denote 

$$
P(x,y)=2-3y,\,Q(x,y)=1.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2-3y)=-3 \\ \frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x}) & =\frac{1}{1}(-3-0) \\  & =-3,\end{aligned}
$$

is a function of $x$ only, we can conclude that an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(\int -3\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(-3x) \\  & ={e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

and by multiplying our differential equation by the integrating factor, we have

$$
I(x)\cdot ((2-3y)\,\text{d}x+\text{d}y)=I(x)\cdot 0
$$

which simplifies as

$$
{e}^{-3x}\cdot ((2-3y)\,\text{d}x+\text{d}y)=0.
$$
